summary:
Jambi is one of Indonesia's provinces and stands under the national framework: the criminal law, the penal code and the administrative rules that govern gender recognition in Jakarta apply in Jambi without local modification. No Jambi-specific ordinance, protection measure or documented incident of anti-trans violence was found in the sources reviewed, so the province's profile is the national one.

The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations. One source records a maximum of one year's imprisonment, and only on complaint by an immediate family member; other reporting gives two years. Prosecutions are reported as selective rather than systematic, but the complaint mechanism means a partner's relatives can initiate a case.

Hostility is embedded in defence policy. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military threats to be monitored and controlled, alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Commentators quoted by a foreign broadcaster state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Physical risk is rising and is not confined to any one province. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender women across Indonesia in a wave of 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage circulated online. A researcher cited in the same reporting documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

Police continue to target LGBT gatherings. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over an LGBTQ community page on Facebook.

Provincial religious law adds a second layer in two provinces only. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, and Aceh's punishments apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025. Neither provision is in force in Jambi, but a visitor travelling onward to Aceh comes under it.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting regulator banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including the dating app Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and recognition are restrictive. Indonesia recognises only "male" and "female" sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
A 2025 Pew survey found that 93% of Indonesians regard homosexuality as morally unacceptable, a figure that frames the social environment a visitor moves through independently of what the law says on any given day.

Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025, indicating sustained official resistance to external scrutiny of its treatment of LGBT people.

The enforcement texture differs by province: Aceh and South Sumatra impose penalties under provincial religious law while the rest of the country relies on national morality provisions and the penal code. Jambi sits in the second group.

Provincial moral laws and Aceh caning remain the enforcement texture cited in regional reporting, and a researcher documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016, so the direction of travel across the archipelago is toward greater public hostility rather than away from it.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for residents requires sex reassignment surgery and approval from a judge, and identity documents can carry only "male" or "female"; there is no third-gender or X marker available.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, at national level or through any Jambi ordinance.

The extra-marital sex provision can be set in motion by a complaint from an immediate family member, which places the exposure inside households as well as in dealings with police.

Residents who publish or share content depicting same-sex relations risk the 2006 pornography statute, and LGBT community pages have already led to arrests; government blocking of apps and sites carrying LGBTQ-related words restricts ordinary online organising.

Indonesia recognises only opposite-sex marriage, so no partner recognition or marital protection is available to same-sex couples in Jambi.
outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty under the 2022 penal code is recorded inconsistently across the sources reviewed: one gives two years' imprisonment, another one year on complaint by an immediate family member. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

No Jambi-specific ordinance, protection measure or documented incident of anti-trans violence was found in the sources reviewed. That is an absence of sourced material, not a finding that no such incident has occurred in the province.

Whether Jambi police have conducted raids on LGBT gatherings, and how the province's authorities implement the October 2025 presidential decree, is not sourced.

The status and fate of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour, and whether it has been enacted, is unresolved in the material reviewed.

Reporting on the July 2026 vigilante wave names Bogor; whether comparable attacks occurred in Jambi during that period is not sourced.
